- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

items.title: We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from ba
items.content:
We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from bacterial life.

Vault particles are a longstanding mystery. They are barrel-shaped objects, among the largest protein structures found in our cells. They were first discovered by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha in 1986, but their function remains unknown.

With Claude, we’ve found results that might bring us closer to solving that mystery.

Until now, vaults were only known in the cells of complex things like animals and plants. We have shown that similar proteins from bacteria (and the viruses that infect them) can also assemble into vaults. Finding the structures in these simpler forms of life may make it easier to investigate their function in our own cells.

For our life sciences team, the project was also a demonstration of the potential (and the limitations) of using AI to accelerate science.

In our full piece, we discuss how Claude was able to dramatically speed up some stages—manually determining the vault particle’s structure would have taken weeks to months of painstaking work, but here it took days. We also discuss how Claude made some simple mistakes along the way, and how we collaborated with our machine learning researchers to address them.

Read more: https://t.co/KowVVCSPp8

New on our Science Blog: How AI is beginning to change scientific modeling.

Scientific models help researchers explain and predict real-world systems—like how a single nerve cell fires, or what happens when neutron stars collide. Recent advances have transformed how scientists fit complex models to data. But scientists still typically write the models manually, and usually need to weigh up several competing versions, each of which might explain the data in a different way.

In a guest post, Jakob Macke, Daniel Gedon, and Stefan Wahl describe how AI is starting to help with these parts of the process. By writing, running, fitting, and revising scientific models as code, AI can explore many possible model structures, and find out which explanations the data support.

items.content:
There are a few notable counter-examples (e.g. HAL) but this is basically right for a lot of pre-2000 sci-fi.

I think getting AI right from e.g. somewhere in the ~1970s would require a fairly complicated set of inferences, probably the biggest things would be:

Image the world in 50 years.
1. "Digital knowledge work / computing". The vast majority of knowledge work (which makes up a very large fraction of the economy) goes digital. As computers get cheaper, much of society’s work happens on screens, over billions of machines in homes and offices.
2. "Internet". Similar to ARPANET (and see Licklider’s “Intergalactic Computer Network” (1963)), this creates demand for a global network of computers where people work, argue, teach, joke, and socialize.
3. "Big data". This creates a very large, compounding repository of digital information, with traces of how people reason, how they create, what they know etc.
4. "Statistical learning". Trying to program intelligence by hand is extremely difficult. But Shannon's n-gram approximations of English (1948) show examples of how language has statistical structure that can be "learned". You could imagine doing so over extensions of cybernetic computing (e.g. in the style of Rosenblatt's Perceptron 1958). So instead of programming thought, we could fit a statistical model to the record.
5. "LLMs". This might lead to something along the lines of ELIZA (1966), but with enough data (per 1-3), and enough compute (see Moore's law 1965), the imitation might become of extreme hight fidelity to the point that it's economically extremely useful.
6. "Scaling laws". These networks may demand a huge amount of data / computing resources and expertise to train. It's plausible that the more of each you have, the better your ELIZA gets. The economics concentrate, where a few organizations build a few minds and then deploy copies of them digitally.

Something like that. Basically, it's a lot of leaps. You have to start with computers, to internet, to big data, to big compute (Moore's law), which then allow large-scale statistical learning approach based on neural networks, and then posit scaling laws, and then imagine the form factor of language models as a lot more sophisticated ELIZA. And you'd have to short everything else, most predominantly I think the idea that we'd figure out how to program robots by hand.

items.title: The era of System One Vision Model is here! Introducing VFlash: parsing the visual world in parallel at unmatched speeds
items.content:
The era of System One Vision Model is here! Introducing VFlash: parsing the visual world in parallel at unmatched speeds for Physical AI.

Most embodied prediction tasks like object localization, robot trajectory planning, and dense 3D motion are fixed-length float vectors. For example, a bounding box is always 6 tokens, a 10-waypoint robot arm trajectory is 54: we know these beforehand. Instead of decoding one token at a time, we can output the entire geometric shape in one go. 

VFlash enables up to 12x faster action decoding and a 5.1x overall robot inference speedup on edge GPUs like the Jetson Thor and DGX Spark. What’s surprising is that it ends up even more accurate than the VLM backbone, with up to 61% lower 3D trajectory error. The intuition is that VFlash avoids the cascading errors of autoregressive decoding, where every coordinate is written in ink and every later point loses the chance to backspace.

Everything that moves will be autonomous, and everything autonomous will need to think on its own chip. The next inference revolution is physical reasoning at the speed of reflex.

And as always, it’s open paper, open source! Link in thread:

items.content:
AI can now help turn a published fix into a working exploit in hours. Patching still takes weeks, and for many old routers, cameras, and supermarket fridges, a fix never arrives.

"So the question isn't how to patch faster. It's how to stop needing to."

Six openings for new cybersecurity companies today, each one making patching "unnecessary, or someone else's job":

1. Live fixes: blocks an exploit on running systems within hours, then has AI write and ship the real code fix

2. An AI first responder: spots attacks without hand-written rules and contains them as they unfold

3. Per-request access: checks every request from a person or their AI agents, with credentials that expire in minutes

4. Proven recovery: keeps restoring your backups in a sealed-off test environment to prove they work, with records insurers will accept

5. An install gateway: holds and sandboxes every package, extension and AI agent tool before it can run

6. Security for the long tail: one managed service for water utilities, clinics and others that will never have a security team

Full piece from a16z's Asaf Ezra and Steph Zhang: https://t.co/y6LXgU1fbi

items.content:
John Somorjai of Salesforce on what kills company acquisition deals, from attrition hiding behind ARR to a veto from the security team:

"It's really important that you're ready and you're organized so that the data is flowing and it doesn't look like you're having trouble getting access to data."

items.title: Launch HN: Rivet (YC W23) – Scale and Orchestrate Agents on S3
items.content:
Launch HN: Rivet (YC W23) – Scale and Orchestrate Agents on S3 Hey HN, this is Nathan and Nicholas from Rivet (https://rivet.dev) – a fast, high-density, and scalable orchestrator for agentic workloads using the actor model. Rather than running a heavyweight sandbox per agent, each agent gets a lightweight actor backed by S3.

Actors provide a long-lived process for long agent turns, in-memory state for context, a WebSocket server for multiplayer, durable SQLite storage backed by S3, and hibernation when idle.

It's a similar model to Cloudflare Durable Objects, but it’s open source and self-hostable.

Here’s a video walkthrough: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3Ev6I7DOV9c

When we went through YC in 2023, we were building infrastructure for multiplayer games like Diep and Krunker. This involved heavily optimizing high-throughput matchmaking, real-time player messages, and blitz scaling. Through that process, we spent a lot of time on workloads where Postgres couldn't keep up with our throughput. We started out by hacking together Lua scripts on top of Redis, but this became too cumbersome to maintain and upgrade. This led us to extend our game server orchestrator to support what we call Rivet Actors today: many lightweight workers with in-memory state and durable storage. By using actors, we were able to serve tens of millions of monthly active users.

As agents grew in popularity, it became clear that running agents in sandboxes is inefficient. Sandboxes are expensive, mostly idle, and slow to start. Developers started using actors because they are far more memory efficient (72 KB baseline for actors vs 512 MB for a minimal sandbox) and fast to start (4.9 ms p99 for actors vs 1.7 s p99 for sandboxes).

For example, Amp is using Rivet to orchestrate multiplayer agents. They originally tried to build on Cloudflare Durable Objects, but couldn’t launch because of the platform’s limitations and unresponsive support. They migrated to Rivet Actors in a weekend and deploy on-prem. Rivet’s flexible architecture lets them adapt it to their own use cases without being constrained by a framework or the memory, storage, and runtime limits of Cloudflare Durable Objects.

Under the hood, Rivet is backed by S3 while maintaining SSD speeds.

Why S3? Previously, Rivet ran on FoundationDB. However, we were surprised to find that companies are storing orders of magnitude more data on Rivet Actors than in Postgres, such as large session transcripts, agent artifacts, and full POSIX filesystems. As their data grew, they had to start paying for SSDs that sat mostly idle with old transcripts. This led us to double down on S3 as our primary storage medium without sacrificing performance. This choice means that data stored on Rivet is 10× cheaper than on EBS gp3 while maintaining SSD speeds.

It’s not as simple as writing data straight to S3. Lots of PUTs for tiny blobs of data are slow and expensive. Instead, we use an SSD tier to optimize speed and cost:

When you write data to an actor’s SQLite database, the write is acknowledged once SSDs in 2 of 3 availability zones have it. Then, the data is batched to S3 in the background. This means that S3 is never on the write path, which lowers latency and cost. When reading data or waking an actor, Rivet reads from SSDs if already cached and falls back to S3 if not. SSD caches can be tuned to meet your needs, giving you configurable tiered storage for your actors.

This architecture lets Rivet provide 1.07 ms durable writes (3 AZ, p99), 1.36 ms reads (p99), and 138 ms reads from object storage (p99).

We’ve spent a lot of time making sure that Rivet can run wherever you need it. Self-hosting requires deploying a single Rust binary with S3 as the only dependency, Rivet Cloud lets you deploy dedicated clusters on AWS or GCP in any region, and BYOC lets us deploy Rivet to your VPC without having to operate it yourself. Rivet also runs identically in local dev as in production, since Rivet is a lightweight binary that runs anywhere

Rivet Actors can be written in TypeScript or Rust. Out of the box, they support agents (Pi Durable), workflows, real-time, multiplayer, running AI-generated code, Durable Streams, and integrations with tools like Vercel’s Eve and Turso. See all of our available guides, or point your agent at them: https://rivet.dev/docs/#guides

Try it out now, by reading our quickstart guides (https://rivet.dev/docs/) or ask your agent: “Run npx skills add rivet-dev/skills, then build a multiplayer chat agent and run it locally.”

We’d love to get feedback on your experience with Rivet! We’re deeply invested in making Rivet an easy-to-self-host, flexible, and efficient way to run agentic workloads.

GitHub: https://github.com/rivet-dev/rivet

Architecture: https://rivet.dev/docs/architecture/

Benchmarks: https://rivet.dev/docs/benchmarking/

Self-hosting: https://rivet.dev/docs/deploy/self-host/

items.content:
If you know me, you'd know I love AI. But I'll never let agents touch my money (my bank, my cards, or my Stripe). That's where I draw a strict boundary.

The reason is simple: the day an agent can move my money is the day I stop knowing where it goes.

And yet, Claude saved me $10,200 a year without access to my bank account or money. Here's how:

Step 1. Go to all your bank accounts apps.
Step 2. Download 12 months of transactions from every bank as CSV files.
Step 3. Put the CSV files in a folder on desktop.
Step 4. Go to Claude. Set it to Opus 5.5 on 'High.'
Step 5. Open the CSV files folder in Claude.
Step 6. Send this prompt (with your context):

"Be my CFO. Find every place I lose money, biggest first. I attached [12] months of transactions from [MY BANKS AND CARDS]. Some accounts are [PERSONAL / BUSINESS]. Remove transfers between my own accounts so nothing counts twice.

List every recurring charge, with its price and next renewal. Ask me 5 to 10 questions before you give advice. Then tell me what to CUT, KEEP, or RENEGOTIATE, with yearly savings. Use code for every number. Never ask for a password or account number."

Step 7. This prompt is not the end. I gave the entire prompt (which actually saved me money) in this free guide: https://t.co/38nzKYzEFG

You will also get the steps on how to turn memory & training off first, or how to make Claude draft the cancel emails for you.

I ran it on my own finances, and I was surprised by what it found. Claude drafted an email to Stripe to reduce my fee from 2% to 1% (worth $10,200 a year) on its own.

But to go a level beyond, you need two extra (still simple) steps:

>A money app you update every month
>Claude drafting every cancel and renegotiation email in your Gmail.

It drafted 21 for me. I just pressed Send. I shared the entire process in the guide.

It works on the free plan. Go here: https://t.co/38nzKYzEFG

items.content:
Here's 4 steps to run an uncensored AI on your own GPU for $0:

I run a local abliterated Gemma 4 for anything I don't want leaving my machine

By the end, you'll know how to:
- run a model which has no refuses
- plug it into Claude Code
- do it all for $0, no API key, no account

So, let's go step by step:

1. Install Ollama

curl -fsSL https://t.co/Xqcu5R7xOu | sh
you want a recent version, older builds don't speak the Anthropic API and don't support Gemma 4

2. Pull the model

ollama pull igorls/gemma-4-12B-it-heretic-GGUF

the biggest mistake people make here is grabbing a random "uncensored" tag with no quality numbers

this one is abliterated with Heretic. refusals went 99/100 → 0/100 at a KL divergence of 0.028 from the original, so you keep almost all of the base model's capability

one thing: it's still Google's Gemma license underneath, fine for personal use, but read the terms before you build a product on it

3. Turn off thinking (the part every other guide skips)

Gemma 4 is a hybrid thinking model and the abliteration targets non-thinking mode

leave thinking on and the reasoning block eats your token budget and the answer gets cut off

ollama run igorls/gemma-4-12B-it-heretic-GGUF

/set nothink
if you're calling the API instead, add "think": false to the request

4. Plug it into Claude Code (OPTIONAL)

ollama launch claude --model igorls/gemma-4-12B-it-heretic-GGUF

or manually:

export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434

export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN=ollama
claude --model igorls/gemma-4-12B-it-heretic-GGUF
two gotchas:

- bump the context first. Ollama defaults to 4k and Claude Code's system prompt alone is bigger than that, so the model never sees its tool instructions. restart the server with OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=32768 ollama serve (setting it in your shell does nothing if Ollama is already running as a service). this needs more VRAM than the 8GB below

- Gemma 4 tool calling is still rough, you should expect some failed edits, imo for serious agentic work use qwen3.5 or glm-4.7-flash instead

What you need:

- 8-12GB VRAM for Q4 (12B)
- ~8GB of disk for Q4, ~13GB for Q8
- more of both if you want a big context
honest take:

- "abliterated" means refusals removed, not quality added. it's still a 12B

- fewer refusals ≠ smarter. for real coding work I still use cloud models
- you own the weights, your prompts never leave the box. that's the actual win
*IMPORTANT: don't use it for anything illegal or harmful. that's on you, not the model

now i'm collecting a list of every uncensored model i'm adding to my local stack and which tasks each one replaces for me

also planning a big "Uncensored 101" article, still figuring out all the angles

save it so you don't lose it

items.content:
Meaghan Choi designs Claude Code at Anthropic. This prompt turns Claude Code into the design partner most solo builders never had.

Most people ask Claude for a screen and judge it from the diff. The build is green, the page looks fine at one width, and nobody ever opens the empty state.

So this prompt makes Claude Code work like a designer who codes. Six passes, in order:

Brief. Directions. Pick. Redline. Polish. Walkthrough.

Brief: one user, one job, one moment that should feel good. Claude waits for your yes before it builds.
Directions: three versions in real code. Closest to the system, half the elements, and the bold one.
Pick: six screenshots side by side, scored on clarity, hierarchy, density and delight. You choose. No blended compromise.
Redline: Claude opens the running page and checks spacing, type scale, contrast, 44px targets, and the empty, loading and error states. Every miss becomes one line in taste.md.
Polish: one fix at a time, with a fresh screenshot after each one.
Walkthrough: keyboard only, text at 200%, dark mode. It reports what it saw on screen, not what the code says.

Every time you correct its taste, the rule goes into CLAUDE.md under ## taste. The next screen starts with all of them.

THE CORE
1. Claude Code · 154,768 stars
the agent that builds, runs and screenshots the screens
https://t.co/VjPQgFV6M1

2. Agent Skills · 188,060 stars
start with frontend-design and webapp-testing
https://t.co/5ZrIsartVF

LET IT SEE THE PAGE
3. Playwright MCP · 39,261 stars
a real browser, real screenshots, real clicks
https://t.co/3m6yorebdC

4. Chrome DevTools MCP · 54,877 stars
console, network and performance traces for the redline pass
https://t.co/C9Myt7PLPP

5. Figma Context MCP · 16,173 stars
hands Claude the layout data instead of a flat picture of the mockup
https://t.co/RAfOXU3tiz

KEEP IT CONSISTENT
6. shadcn/ui · 127,504 stars
components and tokens to reuse before Claude invents new ones
https://t.co/vIeQ13lJOE

7. Storybook · 91,467 stars
every empty, loading and error state in one place
https://t.co/n56BLvVpWc

8. axe-core · 7,769 stars
the contrast and accessibility check behind "AA or better"
https://t.co/wBbgkppaKp

THE CATCH
A green build is not a good screen. Keep the pick and the final yes with a human.

Taste is not a prompt. It is a list of rules you keep writing down.

Fuck dropshipping, Fuck claude code, Fuck building AI startups

it's all for poors

The easiest way to start a business with AI in 2026 is running a faceless page on youtube that posts one surprising tech story every day....

99% of you won't do it because posting daily is too boring

Total tool stack to operate one of them: $[TOTAL]/mo

Claude $[X] (scripts from sources)
ElevenLabs $[X] (AI voice)
Viktor FREE (the AI analyst)
Uploads FREE

That's the entire infrastructure for pages that did 36,000+ views

Move 1. Pick one niche that pays.

Pick a real repeatable page format. AI voice for explainers. Slideshows for carousel pages. Tall pins for Pinterest traffic.

Move 2. Run the 3-part originality check.

Don't post stock clips on day 1. Research for every video. Write your own script. Add a point of view to everything. Then start the real daily posting.

Skip this and you get demonetized for template content

Move 3. Study 5 big pages.

Filter to your niche formats: recaps, demos, surprises, roundups. Skip pages with no repeating series. Borrow the series, not just the headline they already use

Move 4. Write the 60-second Shorts script.

Hook line ("a $60M AI supercomputer just got listed on eBay with $50 shipping"). One story, one specific number. AI voice reading your own lines. Number visible from second one

Move 5. Post one short video a day.

Most will flop. By week 3 we had 1 winner pulling 10,207 views. Part 2 every winner. Drop losers.

Move 6. Hand your numbers to an AI employee first.

Every post in one CSV with views, shares, skip rate and length, read in Slack. 1,239 median under 90s vs about 50.

Drafts your Monday report for approval

Day 1 was 4 views. Week 3 hit 10,207 views. Both pages crossed 36,000 views in the first 3 weeks. Not monetized yet, honest numbers

The math nobody talks about

Dropshipping requires inventory, supplier negotiations, ad spend, returns, customer service. Average margin 4-12%. Average operator burnout: 14 months

Coding with claude requires you to learn how software works, get a job at a tech company that may not exist in 4 years, work 50+ hours/week for $120-180k. Average path to $30k/mo: 7-10 years

Building an AI SaaS requires you to compete with VC-funded teams, scale to product-market fit, fundraise, hire engineers. 90% die in 18 months

Running a faceless AI page requires $[TOTAL]/mo in tools and the willingness to post daily. Our path to 36,000: 3 weeks. Camera needed: Zero

They don't eat. They don't sleep. They don't quit. They don't get hangovers. They don't go through breakups. They don't ask for raises. They don't ghost me on monday morning

They read every post we made in one single pass.
